Highly recommend this. I've been making my own wine for years and a friend of mine makes his own beer. It's a fun hobby once you understand the basics. Fair warning- I poured out three batches of wine before I got the hang of making something drinkable. But the results have been well worth it. I've made about 80 bottles of mead that, IMO, have all tasted better than the $15-$20 bottles I can get at the local market.

I'm really surprised ours turned out so well. We literally took fresh plums, rinsed them in hose water, stuffed them in two carboys, added corn sugar and hose water to target 15% abv, and used champagne yeast plus yeast nutrient mix.

No sulfates, no boiling the must, nothing fancy. One batch went bad but the other was great.

I bet doing things properly and following a recipe would make it even better and improve the yield.

A couple of notes. Personally, I've enjoyed the results using brown sugar more than corn sugar. but YMMV. Champagne yeast is a bit aggressive for me, but if you're going for a high ABV, and 15% is fairly high, then you need something like that to react with all the sugar.

I don't boil the must, either. If I'm using dry yeast, I'll heat water and add the yeast. Stir and pour in. But again- YMMV.

Sulfates are important- it keeps the wine fresh longer. You won't notice the lack right away, but your wine will "skunk" faster. Sometimes, I'll use commercial grape juice. Making sure it's nothing but juice and sulfates is difficult- most aren't. But the nice thing is that the amount of sulfates is regulated by the FDA. Who are probably better at it than I am.

But, yeah. You don't have to make a big production of it to get a drinkable wine.

How hard is it too sit up a still? I kinda want to turn my plum wine into brandy.

Well, depending on where you are, I can recommend the Still Spirits AirStill. I've got one, and if fucking rocks!

Otherwise, I've made one with about a yard of 3/8inch copper tubing, a large pot with a hole in the lid (mine had a removable center handle leaving a hole), an old coffee can, some ice, and some salt dough. Fill the pot with what you want to distill. Seal the lid with salt dough (flour, water, salt). Coil the copper into a cylinder shape that will fit in the old coffee can, punch a hole in the lower side to let one end of the copper through. Run the other end of the copper in an arch to the lid of the pot and dough it in place. Fill coffee can with ice and water, mostly ice. Start up your stove and slowly heat it up. Don't heat it too fast or the lid will come off.

I suggest you look up diagrams online. The rough one I made in about an hour, and most of that was coiling the copper right and sealing the joint where the tube comes through the bottom side of the coffee can. (I used silicone)
